CRIMES AND CRIMINALS.
A horrible triple murder is reported from Dawson, Terrell county, Ga. A negro named Frank Hudson called at the house of an old white man named David Lee, who it was known kept a good sum of money in his house. Finding Lee at home, with a view of decoying him away from the house, he told him that his field fence, a short distance from his residence, was on fire. Lee started for the scene, accompanied by Hudson, who offered to assist him in putting out the flames. The negro, before going, picked up an ax, stating he would probably need it to cut away the burning portion. Soon after leaving the house, and while on the way to the place where the fence was said to be burning, Hudson struck Lee a terrible blow on the head with the ax, splitting his head open and killing him instantly. He then returned to the house, when he killed Mrs. Lee and servant with the same ax, and also struck down with the same weapon another servant girl, leaving her as he supposed in a dying condition. Hudson then robbed the house, getting $500 as the proceeds of his fiendish crime, and left.

Five prisoners in the jail at Hot Springs overpowered an infirm guard and made their escape.

Two men, named Fulsom and Hobbs, murdered John Stewart, of Waldron, Ark., to recover $60 lost at poker. William Massingale gave the alarm, and was shot dead.

Capt. Howgate's system of embozzlement consisted of paying himself for goods which were never really purchased. The detectives found firms in New York who were supposed to have supplied various lots of material who denied receiving either the orders or the money. His embezzlement bids fair to mount up into the hundreds of thousands of dollars. Attorney General McVeagh has caused him to be rearrested and held in $90,000 bail.

—Perry Mason and Alexander Wilson, both colored, confined at Monroe, La., on a charge of murder, were taken thence by a mob of disguised men and hanged.

—A jewelry store at Atlantic City, N. J., was robbed of goods valued at $10,000 while the proprietor was absent for dinner.

—Four saloon keepers connected with the City Council of Omaha have been arrested for violation of the high-license law. The Council refuses to pass an ordinance for the issuing of licenses, and no liquor-dealer has tendered the $1,000 fee.

—An old feud led to a tragedy at Johnston, Edgefield county, S. C. John W. Buzzard and his son attacked J. W. Timmerman with shotguns. Timmerman used a shot-gun in defense. Timmerman was killed, and Buzzard and his son were seriously injured.

—In an affray between Ben Blanton and James Todd, in Cook county, Texas, Todd was shot through the heart, and Blanton had the top of his head shot off.

—The shooting of a Deputy Sheriff at Benson, Arizona, caused the citizens to burn the furniture of a gambling den and order the whole party to leave by first train or be lynched.

The colored people of Galveston have passed resolutions excoriating Governor Roberts for permitting the butchery of innocent negroes by the mob at Orange.

STEPHEN ORNAY, who was arrested in Boston for the embezzlement of money from the German government, has been placed aboard a Hamburg steamer at New York.

The Indiana, Bloomington and Western Railway company offers a reward of $500 for the conviction of the man who tied the boy Cantwell to the track and caused his death by mutilation.

The conspirators among the Cornell crew are said by the Itnaca Journal to have been led by Shinkel, his partners being Michael Casey, a saloon-keeper, and Samuel W. Reed, a wholesale liquor dealer. Shinkel wrote to Casey from London to bet against the crew.

Lucius M. Witham, who was once police captain at Lowell, Mass., but who for sixteen years been a resident of Reedsboro, Vt., was shot dead through a window by some unknown person at night. It is known that his life had been threatened by a neighbor named Calvin Fuller.

Chas. Stockley was executed at Batavia, N. Y., for killing John Wilker, who refused him the hand of his daughter in marriage. Stockley feigned insanity in prison, and it took four strong men to shackle him. His father has not visited him since the murder, and his mother left him with dry eyes after a brief interview.

Sears cut the throat of Sallie Freeman, a yellow girl, because she started for church with a rival. The horrible deed was perpetrated on the sidewalk on Small street, and his victim was a corpse in five minutes from the time of his assault.

On Tuesday morning about 2 or 3 o'clock Gen. C. C. Batterman, late of Virginia City, passed from our midst and went to join the innumerable caravan beyond our ken. He has been in Arizona but a short time and as superintendent of the Head Center mine. During his brief stay, he made himself exceedingly popular and beloved by many. He had lately built himself a house at the mine, his wife had joined him, and he anticipated a pleasant stay in Tombstone, but it was willed otherwise and his kindly heart was stilled forever. Heart disease was the cause of his sudden death. Yesterday his funeral took place, under the auspices of Cochise lodge No. 5, I. O. O. F., which the General had lately organized and almost their first official act was to bury him. The funeral was the largest I have seen during my residence in Tombstone, and spoke volumes for the popularity of a good man. Hic jacet will be written above him and the great selfish world move on as ever. Such are the uncertainties of this life of ours.

There was a rumor last evening that Byrnes, of the top and bottom game, notoriety had been lynched at Benson, but the news was too good to be true and was contradicted by the arrival of that worthy here last night in charge of an officer, booked on a charge of assault to murder, and he now reposes calmly in our jail pending investigation.

Judge W. Earll, of your city, is still confined to his room with a broken arm, but the Doctor says he will be around in a few days. His son Fred, well-known in Tucson, has been visiting him for a few days.

M. Gray returned yesterday from his visit to the scene of the late murder, and reports everything quite. The wild rumor of the vast crowd of determined men going out to avenge the dead men is all bosh. There were eleven men in the party and the object of their trip was to bury the dead—this accomplished they returned—had they encountered the murderers it is possible summary vengeance would have been met out to them, but the idea of doing any thing lawless was ridiculous and the creation of some idle person's fancy.

Mr. Lang, one of the gentlemen of the party, took seven men for the purpose of driving in his cattle, as no less picture ber could do the work. Mr. Gray passed here on his way home, and is expected here to-day; so endeth the first chapter.

Our Hook and Ladder boys exercise every little while, and have got so they can handle the machine very well. News has been received stating the Fire Company's hose and cart was lying at Benson, and it will soon be here, but unless the water company make more rapid progress in getting the fire plugs in position and water turned on, the hose and cart won't prove of any very great benefit in case we should have another fire.

The news from the bonanzas this week is more encouraging than last by reason of the fact that the water has gone down so the mills are running ahead as usual, and the customary amount of work is now being pushed ahead, and the ore teams now plod along freighted with bullion-producing rock.

THE GRAND CENTRAL SOUTH

Just now comes to the front with a good strike and consequently claims the most attention. Dr. Gardiner the superintendent feels justly elated over the successful workings of the past few weeks. The south shaft is now down about fifty-five feet and it was here the new strike has been made. From the top to the bottom of the shaft the ore vein is dintinct and promises well. The vein has now widened out to over four feet and the ore therefrom runs as high as $150 per ton and lower. The east ledge long looked for, has at last been discovered and sinking commenced thereon. They have a good ledge here also and quartz vein. The knowing ones are elated over this latter discovery because it demonstrates that they are continuations of the Grand Central and hence liable to be very rich. The main working shaft, as well timbered a piece of work, by the way, as one would wish to see, lies about midway between these ledges, and this will develop well when drifts are run and general work commences. At the present writing the prospects of this property are most flattering, and I only hope that time and development will not disappoint the expectations of its fortunate owners and genial superintendent.

THE ALTA,

Lying about 1000 feet to the west of the Grand Central, and midway between it and the Lucky Cuss, is bounded by the Emilie, Mayflower and Independence, all three of which have good ledges and plenty of ore. The Alta was incorporated in California in April last, and is now known as the Horseshoe Mining Company, with Mr. Alf. Tregedga as superintendent. Work was commenced in April last, immediately after the incorporation, and pushed rapidly ahead. A visit to the property shows the shaft now down 156 feet, and three shifts at work. The shaft is near the East Side line, and in its descent has cut three ledges, carrying ore ranging from $000 to $100 per ton. The shaft is now in very hard rock, and work is necessarily a little slow. The quality of rock is dolomite impregnated with pyrites, carrying gold. They are working now to strike the main ledge, some 300 feet from the shaft, and dipping east. They do not hope to reach it under 250 or 300 feet. A whim, blower, etc., are incentives to labor, and the proper men to push it, should soon show something that will repay labor.

THE THOMAS HERESY CASE.
CHICAGO, Aug. 26.—Dr. Willings has appointed the Rev. J. C. Steoughton, of Aurora, to assist Drs. Hatfield and Jewett in the prosecution of the case of the Rev. Dr. Thomas who is charged with heresy.

AN ABANDONED WOMAN KILLED.
St. PAUL, Minn., Aug. 26.—Kate Hutton, a notorious woman, was shot fatally about midnight by "Ed" Wright, her negro paramour, with whom she was living on the prairie north of the city. Wright claims that the shooting was accidental.

POISONING HIS ENTIRE FAMILY.
WAUKESHA, Wis., Aug. 26.—One Howard, living in Delafield, ten miles north of this place, poisoned his entire family yesterday, and his wife and two children have died. An ungovernable temper and domestic troubles are the causes assigned for the deed.

INDIANA CROP PROSPECTS.
INDIANAPOLIS, Ind., Aug. 26.—W. H. Ragan, president of the State Board of Agriculture, says that the crops in the central and southern portions of the State will not be one-half the average, but in the northern part there will be about a two-thirds crop. All the cereals are suffering in a like degree, and if there is not a heavy rain in a very few days in many counties of the State nearly all the corn will be cut up for fodder. The wheat prospect is bad, and there is very little hay. Fruit, especially apples, promised well, but in the last few weeks the drought has had a telling effect upon them, and they will fall below the average.

Tar, Feathers and Murder.
DETROIT, Mich., August 27.—A negro, named Charles Dow, was murdered on Tuesday last in the township of Riley, Clinton county. The negro had many enemies, although not of a quarrelsome disposition. It was generally believed in the neighborhood, however, that he abused his wife and was cruel to his stock, and abut a month ago a party of men broke into his house in the middle of the right, bound, gaged, tarred and feathered him, and threatened to take his life if he did not change his course. On the night in question his wife was absent. His house was again visited on Tuesday night, but by whom is not known. His body was found the next morning hanging in the barn, with a cut over the left eye, penetrating the skull, and sufficient to have caused instant death. There was also a cut on the back port of his head. One leg was dislocated and his back was badly bruised, indicating a terrible struggle. The body was covered with blood.

Tragical Tales.
A dispatch from Brackett, Texas, dated the 26th inst., says: "While four horse thieves, belonging to an extensive gang which have been operating along the Rio Grande for a long time, were being brought to this place yesterday in charge of officers, they were attacked near the town of Dolores, and all the thieves killed."

At Forest City, Ark., on the night of the 27th inst., Lute Wallace invited S. C. Apperson, city marshal, to take a cigar, and while standing at the corner of the saloon Apperson drew a revolver and said: "I think I will shoot you." Wallace, thinking he was jesting, replied, "Shoot away." Apperson was killed for the murder, for the two men were apparently on the murder, the best of terms.

In a street brawl at Silverton, Col., on the 27th., D. G. Ogsbury was killed by roughs.

Charles Dew, a negro, was murdered at his house in Riley township, Clinton county, Mich., on the night of the 23d inst. He was quarrelsome and had abused his wife. Several days ago unknown men men tarred and feathered him.

While James Boyd, of Owensville, Ky., was watching at the bedside of his sick sister, Mrs. McClure, some unknown person person through the window at Boyd. The shock caused Mrs. McClure's death.

A man named Holt was killed at Washington Springs, Chickasaw Nation, on the 26th inst. A dispute over a game of cards.

A gang of desperadoes who had been committing lawless acts in Dangerfield, Titus, Hopkins, Hunt and Trayson, Texas, were pursued by citizens who succeeded in killing one of the outlaws.

Ben Blanton, ex-sheriff of Cook County, had a difficulty with a man named James Todd, who had been a witness against him, and each vowed wengeance on the other. The men met and began shooting at once and both were instantly killed.

John Hermann, a livery stable keeper, and formerly city marshal of Deshler, O., was shot and instantly killed by Peter Cole, a drayman. The killing is the result of a long-standing feud between these two men.

Unknown parties entered the jail at Monroe, La., on the morning of the 23d inst., and secured Perry Mason and Alex. Wilson, (colored) charged with murder, and hanged them.

A tragedy occurred about ten miles from Edgefield County, S. C., on the 24th inst., between J. W. Buzzard and his son and J. W. Timmerman, in which Timmerman was killed and Buzzard and his son seriously injured. An old feud was the cause of the affair. The weapons used were double-barreled shot-guns.

An unknown assassin killed Alderian Pitts, a wealthy and highly respected farmer of Rutherford County, Penn., on the 22d inst. It is thought the cause of the killing originated from a divorce suit instituted some time since between Pitts and his wife.

A teamster named House and Cal Hatcher, a hackman, had a quarrel at Kansas City, Mo., on the 22d inst., about temporary shed room occupied by teams, and House shot Hatcher through the abdomen. House escaped and is still at large. Hatcher will die.

Two desperadoes named Folsom and Hobbs, having lost money in a gambling place at Waldron, Scott county, Texas, returned to the place the following night and shot John Stewart the keeper of the place. Billy Messingale who was visiting the Stewart family received a ball through the head, and will die.

Orange, Texas, is in a ferment, owing to recent lawless acts, and the citizens have thus far hanged six miscreants—Bob and Sam Saxon and four negroes. At last accounts Charles Delno was about to be tried by a "Kangaroo" court of lynchers and the county is being secured by regulators.

MICHIGAN.

Jaaper Cross, an old jeweler at Adrian has failed. Liabilities $15,000. Assets $9,000.

John Berry of Battle Creek, was accidentally shot and killed at Armenia, N. Y.

James Howes of Battle Creek, was killed at Muskegon while coupling care.

Mrs. McKane was seriously injured at Flint by being thrown from a carriage, the horse becoming frightened at a passing elephant.

Percy, a six years old son of Richard Emmons of Cassopolis, fell from a load of lumber, and one of the wheels passed over his breast, killing him instantly.

Base Ball—Chicago 8, Detroit 6. Twelve innings.

Michael Firnane, County Prosecuting Attorney, and ex-President of the Detroit board of education, died at Minneapolis, aged 30.

Fifty of the Chinese students recalled by the government passed through Detroit on the 23rd, on their way home.

Postmaster Vincent of Lapeer, had his farm, barn and contents burned by tramps. Loss $3,000. No insurance.

Jas. G. Wright of Albion is dead, age 60.

Henry McCormick held at East Sagliuw for a Canadian murder in 1870 is to be extradited.

A man giving his name as Albert Smith hired a horse and buggy from Tiffany, a Dundee livery man, and was arrested at Monroe the following day after having sold the rig for $49.

George C. Collins, once a prominent business man in Ypsilanti, has just died at the county house. He was sent there some four months since, his complaint being softening of the brain caused by drink.

W. P. Andrus, state senator from Kent county in 1877 was being taken to the insane asylum at Kalamazoo, when he escaped near Battle Creek and at last reports had not yet been heard from.

A new house just built by Alphonso Hutchins on his farm near Battle Creek has been destroyed by fire with all its contents. The fire is supposed to have been set by a tramp. The loss is $4,000, with an insurance of $1,200 in the Farmers' mutual.

A collision on the D. L. & N. R. R. near Portland wrecked two freight trains and delayed travel several hours.

Jacob Ranswiler, a German about 50 years of age, committed suicide at Albion by taking Paris green. He was intemperate.

Base ball—Detroit 7, Chicago 5.

Chas. Dew, a negro, living in the township of Riley, was murdered by blows upon the head with some sharp instrument and afterwards hanged in his own barn, the whole being apparently done in cold blood. Dew was a small man and not of a fighting disposition, but he had many enemies. It was charged that he abused his wife and was cruel to his stock, and about three weeks ago a party of men forced his door one night, took him out and bound, gagged and "arred and feathered him, and threatened his life if he did not change his course. He was found dead in his barn. There is no clue to his murderers.

E. O. Shaw, of the Newaygo Republican and postmaster of the place, took poison with suicidal intent. He had been absent for a week or more in Chicago, and as supposed, had been indulging quite freely. He is expected to recover.

A young man named Alexander Cofferen of Elk township, was lost off the steamer M. D. Ward at Marine City last night with a brother. They lay down on the deck aft to go to sleep and in the morning were missing. A woman on the boat reports having heard a noise and seen an object in the water while the boat was at the dock a. Marine City and saw it sink, but did not report the fact until morning, when the boat was searched for the Cofferens. Both men were intoxicated.

Dr. Malcolm Mc. Vicar, for the past year principal of the state normal school at Ypsilanti, has accepted the professorship of New Testament interpretation in Toronto university, made vacant by the death of the Rev. John Torrance.

A 6-year-old son of Oliver Shampine fell into a vat of hot brine at Winsor & Co.'s salt block, Post Auston, and died the next day.

Monroe county veterans to the number of 300 attended the reunion at Monroe.

Messrs. Westbrook Divine and Thomas F. Moore, of the board of managers of the state house of correction at Ionia, failing to resign their offices in response to a suggestion of the governor, were yesterday peremptorily removed by him. Joseph T. Escott of Big Rapids, Abraham H. Piper of Lapeer, and George W. Buckingham of Flint were appointed as a new board, their duties to commence August 31.

There is a general strike of saw mill men at Oscoda, in this state, and all the mills are stopped. The strikers interfered with men wishing to work, and an attempt by Sheriff King with three deputies to arrest some of the offenders caused a riot in which the sheriff shot one man in the hip. At last accounts there were 700 men parading the streets, with great excitement and fear of further collisions. The men struck for a reduction of time to 11 hours.

A. M. Flint and Andrew Hardy of Nashville, have been bound over for trial on a charge of bribery by Justice Greenfield at Hastings.

Mrs. James Geer of Lapeer fell forward in her chair and instantly expired. Heart disease.

Miss J. A. King, for the past ten years superintendent of public schools at Charlotte, has accepted the chair of history in the state normal school Ypsilanti.

As Peter P. Greiner of Mt. Clements, and a party of his friends were returning from an excursion to Lake St. Clair, his son Bertie, a lad 7 years old, while playing about the bow of the boat, fell overboard and was drowned. The body has been recovered.

The contract for the erection of the new school house at Portland has been awarded to J. H. Hoskine of Grand Rapids for $9,877.

Four boys who were arrested for breaking into a Chicago and Grand Trunk freight car at Port Huron have escaped. Two of them got out of the city jail one night, and the remaining two took their departure the following night.

The Michigan College of Medicine at Detroit has decided to meet a want which the rapid growth of the city demands, and will at once provide an ambulance for the use of the city on the plan of the public ambulances of New York. The vehicle is built and furnished with all the needful appliances, including medicines, stimulants, mattress, bandages, plaster etc. It will be manned by a skillful attendant and a driver, and will be continuously on duty within telephonic call by the police or any other citizen.

President Garfield is still living. His pulse has registered as high as 138 and his condition is exceedingly critical. Enemata have been again resorted to and they are highly stimulated and frequently administered. It is hoped by this to arrest the continued sleepiness that is considered an undesirable symptom. The inflamed gland is discharging through the left ear. The most serious results are anticipated, though all hope is not abandoned by the attending physicians.

The "Western Michigan Farmers Club" organized at Grand Rapids.

Base Ball—Detroit 9; Chicago 1.

NEWS OF THE WEEK.
MICHIGAN.
The body of Ex-alderman Schultz of Detroit was found in the river. He had been missing for several days.

The Swedish church at Muskegon and its contents, valued at $1,500 was entirely destroyed by fire. It was partially insured.

Daniel Everett of Girard township, had his barn and sheds, with all their contents, burned loss about $1,500; insured for $1,000.

Jos. Kunderhlot, aged 18, a butcher living at Jackson was drowned in Round lake by the capsizing of a boat.

John O. Seffron an old actor, died at the Franklin House Detroit.

Stephen Chalfield, an intemperate painter of Albion, suicided by taking laudanum.

The house, barn and contents belonging to Lan West, at Orion, caught from a marsh which was fired by a passing engine and was burned. Loss, $1,200; insurance, $500.

Mrs. Tyrrell, an old resident of Kalamazoo, died at that place aged 92 years.

Burglaries broke into the safe of C. S. Crandali's grocery store at Harbor Springs and escaped with about $400.

While a steam-thresher was running on the farm of John Welch of Sunfield, sparks set fire to a straw stack, which burned, together with a barn and contents, and adjoining buildings. Loss, $1,200; insured in the Continental. The woods near by caught fire, and it was with great difficulty that a general conflagration was prevented.

John Berry, formerly of Brockway Center, St. Clair county, was found dead in the woods near one of Ward's camps, and was brought down to Ludington for interment.

Reed City is to have water works.

The board of officers appointed to select the companies of state troops to go to Yorktown, have designated the following: 1st regiment Co. A., Ann Arbor; Co. B., Adrian; 2nd regiment, Co. B., Grand Rapids; Co. G., Ionia; 3rd regiment, Co. D., Bay City; Co. E., East Saginaw.

The forest fires now raging in the eastern part of the state nearly equal those of 10 years ago, and in some places are reported as even worse. There has been a frightful loss of life, just how large cannot be told. A number of horrible deaths are reported at Richmondville, including those of three persons roasted alive in a well. The total number of deaths thus far reported is about 20, and it seems likely that the end is not yet. A woman in Sanilac county locked her two children in the house to go for help against the approaching fire, and returned to find that the house had burned and her children had perished in it. A great many people are fleeing to the lake shore to save their lives. The fires appear worst in Saginaw, Tuscola and Sanilac counties, but are breaking out at many points. Several villages are burned and many others threatened. The fires sweep over farms so as to kill even the pigs and chickens, and a great many families are left entirely destitute and must be aided at once.

J B. Wright & Co.'s planing mill at Port Huron has been burned together with a large amount of dressed lumber. Loss $20,000. Insurance $3,000.

John D. Bennett of Palmer Station, was committed at Hastings in default of bail, on a charge of obtaining goods under false pretenses.

Hon. John M. Harris, Judge of the Probate Court, Grand Rapids, is sued for breach of promise by Miss Hattie Holcourt. Damages claimed $10,000.

The new state asylum is to be located with special reference to the requirements of a distinct northern district.

Samuel Massey's saw and shingle mill, located one mile south of McBrides, was burned. Loss $3,000; insurance $2,000.

It is impossible to at present define the extent of the destruction of life and property by the forest fires. Huron and Sanilac counties may be said to be devastated. Reports are contradictory and unsatisfactory, communication being in many instances completely cut off. A great loss of life has certainly occured. Probably 200 is much below the aggregate. The tales of suffering and death are harrowing in the extreme.

The Michigan forest fires prove to be in destruction of life and properly the greatest calamity of the year. The lives lost are estimated at 200 at the lowest, and reports indicate that the figure is likely to be considerably higher. The great disaster was confined almost exclusively to Sanilac and Huron counties. One man traveling about the burnt district is said to have seen the bodies of 116 persons killed by the fire. Forty-five bodies have been found in a single village. The towns back from the shore in Sanilac and Huron counties, from which little has before been heard, are found to have suffered terribly, although no detailed reports are yet given. Through great districts the destruction is complete, and the fire is ended. The sufferings among those who escaped with their lives is severe and widespread, and urgent calls for aid are heard upon every hand. Hundreds and thousands of people, many of these but yesterday well-to-do, are flocking into villages entirely destitute and fairly naked and hungry. In the Saginaw Valley the fires are suiciding, and in some localities rains have ended all danger.

Hulbert Hall of Clio is held for an assault with intent to kill John Z. Richards whom he dangerously injured.

F. D. Lacey's shingle mill at Nirvana was entirely destroyed by fire. Loss $2,500; no insurance.

Base ball—Detroit 6, Cleveland 4.

As later reports come in the worst fears in regard to the Michigan fires are realized. A great tract in Sanliac and Huron counties, 100 miles long on the shore and 20 to 60 miles deep, is mostly burned over, involving a loss of life estimated at from 300 to 1,000, and of property to the extent of millions. Many of the details are almost too horrible for belief. The call for help grows more and more urgent, and already a great many thousand dollars are subscribed, and the whole country is becoming aroused to the work.

The body of Thos. Green, who disappeared from Coldwater, about three months since, has been found hanging to a tree in the outskirts of that city.

Mrs. Galen Johnson was scalded at Fenton by the bursting of a can of tomatoes that she was putting up.

There are 12 girls at the reform school for girls at Adrian.

Robertson Culbertson, a pioneer of Lenawee county, died at Clinton September 2. He came to Tecumseh from Groveland, N. Y., 45 years ago.

The relatives of Mrs. Caroline Lusk assembled on Sept. 1 at the residence of Samuel Sudborough, two miles northeast of Adrian, to celebrate Mrs. Lusk's 90th birthday. Four generations were present to do her honor.

The Macomb county court-house is nearly completed and will cost some $30,000. It is said that the contractor will be out of pocket some $3,000.

The parties who tarred and feathered Dew, the colored man who was murdered in Biley, Clinton county, a few weeks ago, have been discovered. A. W. Burrett confesses to being a party to the crime, and implicates seven others besides himself. The murder is still abroad.

Startling Revelations in the History of a Bank.

DENVER (Col.), April 12th.—This morning's News contains startling revelations concerning the history of the President and Board of Directors of the Commercial Bank of this city, which was incorporated on the 21st of last February, with a capital of $100,000 and a suppositional reserve fund of an equal amount. The Board of Directors consists of James L. Van Woert, President; Ellen M. Van Woert, Cashier; Pliny S. Rice, Horace W. Colton and P. T. Smith, Directors. The News says that these people evidently had plaas well advanced towards perpetrating a gigantic swindle, and continues substantially as follows: Van Woert, the President, served six years in the Penitentiary at Charlestown, Mass., for passing counterfeit money in 1860. He subsequently started a bogus bank at Winsted, Conn., with himself as President and his wife Cashier. He disappeared, leaving many debts, and swindling hundreds of people. Indictments for bigamy are pending over his head, and he is accused of many other crimes. His associates are, with the exception of Colton and Smith, of the same stripe. Rice is well known to the police, and there is an indictment against him at Leadville for obtaining money under false pretenses. Van Woert was to leave today for New York to place $500,000 of stock belonging to the Longmont, Midd'e Park and Pacific Railroad.

The Missouri River.
COUNCIL BLUFFS, April 12th.—The river is now within its banks. No damage has occurred in the city.
YANKTON (Dakota), April 12th.—The overflowed water of the Missouri is gradually subsiding, though the ice is piled to a height of ten to thirty feet along the bank and on the bars and bottoms. Yankton is filling with refugees from the lowlands, and the people are doing their best to care for them, but outside help is needed.

Winter Still Lingering.
POUGHKEEPSIE (N. Y.), April 12th.—A heavy snow-storm prevails along the Hudson. Several inches of snow has already fallen.
MILFORD (Pa.), April 12th.—A heavy snow-storm prevails here. The forest fires will be checked. Snow and hail has been falling since 6 o'clock.
ST. LOUIS, April 12th.—The Republican's Duquoin, Ill., special says: A shower of sulphur fell here during the rain-storm last night.
MEMPHIS, April 12th.—The Appeal's Hernando, Miss., special says: A severe wind-storm passed over the country north of Hernando this afternoon. Dr. Landerdale and wife were severely injured, and several negroes are reported killed; but owing to the swollen condition of the creeks it is impossible to obtain fuller particulars. Hernando is twenty miles south of Memphis.

End of Hattie Deuel's Fast.
Iowa City (Ia.), April 12th.—During the twenty-four hours preceding her death Miss Deuel drank no water, it seeming to sicken her. Her pulse in the morning was imperceptible, and her respiration thirty-five per minute. She was able to communicate with her friends by means of her fingers. She said she was not hungry. Her last moments were very peaceful, and her mind clear.
Iowa City, April 12th.—Hattie Deuel, who died at noon yesterday, was buried this afternoon. Immediately after her death a post mortem examination was made by Dr. Cowperthwaite, Dean of the Homeopathy Department of the University. Not a drop of blood was found in the body. The body weighed 45 pounds. The stomach was also void of any substance. No further analysis has yet been made public.

DOMESTIC INTELLIGENCE.
The large jewelry store of William Wise, in Brooklyn, N. Y., was burglarized a few nights ago. Six large holes were bored in a safe containing $60,000 worth of diamonds, but the steel plates broke the drill. Another safe, weighing 400 pounds, was lifted out of the wall by jackscrews, and robbed of 100 watches, valued at $5,000.

Ex-Attorney General Devens has been re-appointed to the Supreme bench of Massachusetts.

J. L. & L. F. Kuntz, the well-known lager-beer brewers of New York, have made an assignment to their father, their liabilities being $315,000.

Jay Gould has bought Col. Tom Scott's interest in the Texas Pacific railroad.

James O'Brien, better known as Bob Lindsay, pleaded guilty in a New York court to perjury in the famous Morey trial, and was sentenced to State prison for eight years.

West.

The conductors and drivers on the West Division Railway Company, of Chicago, struck for an advance of 20 per cent. in their pay. Over half the city was deprived of street-car facilities for thirty-six hours, and people had to foot it to and from their places of business. The sympathies of the community were with the strikers, and the corporation finally yielded to the demands of the employes.

A strike of the journeymen carpenters of Cincinnati resulted in the concession of $2.25 per day by 125 builders.

Ah Luck, a Chinaman, was hanged at Nevada City for the murder of a countryman.

Col. M. C. Garber, Postmaster at Madison, Ind., and proprietor of the Courier, died from a paralytic stroke.

Great activity is apparent in the work of grading the Northern Pacific up the valley of the Yellowstone, where 3,000 men will soon be employed, preference being given those who intend settling in the region.

Under the escort of Senators Conkling, Jones, Logan and others, the remains of the late Senator Matt H. Carpenter, of Wisconsin, arrived at Milwaukee on the 9th inst., and were formally delivered to the Governor and Legislature of the State that had elected Mr. Carpenter to the Senate, by Senator Conkling, in behalf of the Senatorial committee. The iron-works of C. & G. Cooper & Co., at Mount Vernon, Ohio, were destroyed by fire, causing a loss of $150,000.

Gen. Ben Spooner died at Lawrenceburg, Ind., last week. He was Colonel of the Eighty-third Indiana in the war, and lost a leg at Kenesaw. He was born in Mansfield, Ohio; aged 58.

Mrs. Charles Ballou, of Saranac, Mich., known as the "Mammoth Queen," is dead. When traveling with exhibitions she weighed 570 pounds, but wasted away to 400.

Mark Beaubien, doubtless the most noted of all the pioneers of Chicago, who kept the first hotel and ran the earliest ferry across the Chicago river, died at Kankakee, Ill., a few days ago, aged 81 years. David McKee, another of the early pioneers of Chicago, has also passed away, at the age of 80.

Sioux City dispatches of the 14th inst. represent that snow covers the prairies to the depth of one to three feet, and farmers in that section cannot commence plowing for several weeks. An aid society has been formed to distribute relief in the flooded districts, where the destitute number over 5,000. A Yankton dispatch of the 15th states that twenty families residing at a bend in the Missouri river fifteen miles below Yankton were imprisoned by fields of heavy ice. A colony of 130 people, who had been surrounded by water at Mayville for two weeks, had been rescued. Two relief parties were endeavoring to reach Meckling, where fifty persons were imprisoned by fields of ice from five to twenty feet high. Probably 8,000 settlers have been rendered destitute on the Dakota bottoms.

Charles Marmon, a Leadville stage-driver, entered the theater at Durango, Col., and, without provocation, killed one man and wounded another, both strangers to him. He was hanged by vigilantes.

The annual report of the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe road shows gross earnings of $8,556,975 and a net income of $4,213,770. The length of the road is 1,539 miles, and its funded debt $15,873,000.

At a short-horn sale in Waukegan, Ill., one heifer brought $4,230, and another $2,250.

South.

Three horse-thieves were "summarily disposed of by the vigilantes of Johnson county, Tex.

Four inches of snow fell in Northern Virginia on the night of April 8.

M. W. Gary, a cavalry officer in the Confederate army, and always prominent in law and politics, died at Edgefield, S. C.

A party of armed and masked men rode into Toledo, Ark., at daybreak, surrounded the Court House, broke into the Treasurer's office, and stole about $10,000. They then re-mounted and escaped.

Deputy United States Marshal Seagreaves was recently assassinated and robbed in Macon county, Tenn.

A negro woman was lynched at Martin's Depot, S. C., for attempted arson.

A tornado near Hernando, Miss., demolished many houses, killed three persons and wounded eight others.

A fearful hail-storm visited the town of Fayetteville, Ark., inflicting damage to property estimated at $15,000.

Half the peach crop in Middle and Southwestern Georgia has been killed by frost; the fig-trees are dead, and plums badly injured.

The notorious James brothers are living near Andersonville, Ky.

Heavy frosts have prevailed throughout Texas, and considerable damage has been done to the corn, cotton, fruit and vegetable crops.

Mary A. Murray, an employe of the Baltimore Postoffice, sued Postmaster E. B. Tyler for $20,000 damages for an indecent assault upon her. The jury gave her $5,000.

On last Sunday night Jas. H. Smith, who lives on the Short Line railroad, had seven head of fine cattle killed by a train. There ought to be something done to protect the farmer's stock.—Litchfield Sunbeam.

MR. R. CAMPBELL comes out this week with one of the very best of his productions. Mr. C. is a poet of recognized ability, and his poems are well worth reading.

We learn from the Sunbeam that the spotted fever, which has raged on Short creek in Grayson county for a month or so past, has about subsided. Several persons have died, however.

A REDUCTION of one dollar per day has been made in the wages of store-keepers and gaugers by the Commissioner of Internal Revenue. The pay has hitherto been four dollars per day.

The New York Central railroad has on the lowest average 160 trains per day which leave the starting station nine minutes a part. And yet it is said that another road is needed through New York State.

PROCEEDINGS have been instituted against Irvine & Long, contractors on the Lexington & Big Sandy railroad, for cruelty to convicts which were employed on the road during the winter. The stories concerning their mistreatment are fearful. Irvine and Long have both left the country.

ST. NICHOLAS for May is on our table and we find it to be filled with the usual quantity of good things for the little folks. Children of a larger growth may also read it with interest and profit. The subscription price is $3 per year, Scribner & Co., publishers, 743 Broadway, New York.

THE Pink Cottage faith cure still creates considerable excitement near Stanford, Ky. It is reported that many persons have been cured of severe chronic diseases by the sole influence and power of faith and prayer. "Have faith and pray to God" is all the prescription that is used.

THE manner of taking the census of Great Britain is rather curious. It was finished in one night's time by leaving all the necessary blanks at every house in the kingdom and having them filled by a certain hour the next morning. The entire population of England, Scotland and Ireland is probably about 37,000,000.

ANOTHER of the rogues connected with the Star-route swindle is Hon. Mr. Dorsey, Ex-Senator from Arkansas. He is, as are most all the rascals, a darling of the Republican party and one of their shining lights. Not one in all the party can distribute money in a campaign more dexterously or to better advantage than he, and therefore the majority of his party will stand up for him.

ANOTHER Breckenridge boy has risen to distinction, this time by falling from the drop of an impromptu gallows. In other words Reed Moorman one of the most desperate outlaws of the West, was hung by a mob in Durango, Colorado, last week, for the murder of an innocent man. He was a son of John Moorman, deceased, of Owensboro, but was raised in Breckenridge county.

A BURGLAR entered the post-office at Princeton several nights since, and was making out quite a little account with the Government when Mr. Sasseen, the post-office clerk, returned from a show and found him at work. When he found out that he was discovered he made a break for and through the glass door, carrying the whole door out with him. Sasseen fired a shot at him as he ran, but without effect.

PARDONER BLACKBURN has at last opened or rather shut up on the remission-of-fines business in the case of liquor dealers. The petitions of violators of the law continue to come in as also do those of the law-abiding people of the State and as the last-named form the larger and more respectable portion of the inhabitants he is forced, though perhaps against his will, to listen to them. This is pretty late in the day to begin a reform but better late than not at all.

We have just received the first issue of the Litchfield Sunbeam, a paper edited and published at Litchfield, Ky., by Claude J. Yager, formerly of this place. Mr. Yager is to be congratulated on the neat typographical appearance of his paper and we wish him the success he deserves. It requires no small amount of pluck and energy to start a paper where several others have failed, but we feel that the new venture will come out all right. Grayson county badly needs a paper and if her citizens know their interest and watch it the Sunbeam will never be shut out by the clouds of obscurity.

MEASLES rages in Three Forks vicinity.—Bowling Green Democrat. Tackle him, "Tip."

THE Grand Duke Nicholas, of Russia, has been sentenced to imprisonment for life for complicity in the murder of the late Czar.

THE Huntsville (Ala.) Herald says that Republicans give the black man taffy and the white radicals get all the turkey. The editor is a colored man and knows how it is hippish.

We have an able article in type from the pen of "W. C. C." in reply to the article on "Old Fogyism" by "Enterprise." We regret being unable to publish it. Read it next week.

The article on our fourth page should have been credited to the Princeton Banner. It is one of the best things we have seen, and the only one by an ex-Confederate, on the anniversary of President Lincoln's assassination. Be sure to read it.

MESSRS. Riley & Gordon, have taken possession of the remains of the defunct Hawesville Plaindealer and will on the 7th inst. begin the publication of the Democrat at that place. We anxiously await the first issue.

WILL S. HAYS, of the Courier-Journal and author of that once popular ballad, "Mollie Darling" and 350 others of more or less note, is a candidate for Mayor of Louisville. He will undertake to sing the city into a healthy condition physically, financially and otherwise.

Four little boys were killed by a single flash of lightning in Louisville on Thursday of last week. They were returning from school together when they met their fate. They were buried on Saturday and the funeral procession is said to have been the largest ever seen in Louisville.

On our first page you will find an ably written article by "Vindex" in reply to "W. C. C." on the school question. These gentlemen know how to carry on a controversy through the columns of a newspaper and are thoroughly conversant with the question which they are discussing.

Poor little Mahone is between two fires in the Senate. If he votes with Conkling against Robertson the Administration will be perfectly certain to shut down on him, and if he votes for Robinson's confirmation the crested jay-hawk will kick against every thing that is done by or for Mahone.

The Evansville Courier thinks that the prohibition ticket will be hard to beat next year. It says that they have carried their first point—that of bringing it to a vote of the people, and that the first point was the hardest. It is to be hoped that they will not make such a botch of a job as was made in Kansas.

JOSEPH ARMSTRONG and his four sons were taken from Todd county to the penitentiary on a life-time sentence last week. The crime for which they suffer was the murder of Wm. Sweeny, in Todd county, on the seventh of July last. The evidence was purely circumstantial, but was sufficient to justify the heavy sentence passed on them.

THE deadlock in the Senate is about to be broken at last. Senator Miller last week notified Dawes that if the Republicans did not move for an executive session immediately he would vote with the Democrats as he considered it a duty to remove the obstructions in the way of business. Several other members of the party are becoming dissatisfied but none of them seem to want to be the first to say quit.

Of Serving Murderers-The Sheriff and Police Officers Have a Hard Fight.
CHICAGO. Oct. 2. A special dispatch from Bloomington, Ill., gives graphic details of the lynching of the convict, Chas. Pierce, last night. Some of the best citizens were in the front ranks of the lynchers. Business men cheered and encouraged the lynchers, and the women waved their handkerchiefs. For two hours the sheriff, with all his force, the police force and other officials, stood at the jail door and fought and plead with the infuriated crowd. When the murderer was raised the first time, officer Bailey imperilled his life by running in and cutting the rope, attempting to repeat this he came near being killed. The officers called out the fire department to quell the riot by throwing water on the crowd, but cries of "cut the hose," convinced them that that would not do, and the steamers went back. The ringing of the fire bells called out hundreds more and made things more exciting. Despatches passed between Governor Cotton and Lieut. Governor Hamilton, and the sheriff was directed to call on the militia, but it was known that the militia could not be assembled. Fifer, formerly State's attorney, and R. B. Porter, State attorney did all in their power to quiet the mob, promising them that the murderer should be tried and punished, but their pleadings and promises were hooted at. "Justice and the courts are a farce: we have seen to much of court quibblings and the like," were thrust at the officers.

BLOOMINGTON, Oct. 2.—The following is another version of the lynching at about 6:30 this evening: Ted Franks, the jailor, was shot and killed by a prisoner, Charles Pierce, alias Howlett, incarcerated for horse stealing. The jailor went to change the prisoner from one cell to another, having a revolver in his pocket, and no coat on. He went to unlock the cell door, when the prisoner seized the revolver and shot the jailor in the back. The jailor then turned round and was shot in the shoulder. The third shot pierced his heart. The other prisoners seized and held the murderer. The news spread like wild fire, and by 8 o'clock the jail was surrounded by 5,000 men, women and boys, demanding the murderer. The Sheriff and police, summoning a strong force, did all in their power; but at nine o'clock the mob gained an entrance, after nearly tearing down the jail. They put a rope around the prisoner's neck and dragged him through the howling crowd to the nearest tree, where he was soon dangling, a corpse. His shrieks were drowned in the loud cheers and yells of "Hang him!" Some of the best citizens were in the front. Business men cheered and encouraged the lynchers; women cheered and waved their handkerchiefs when the hope was strongest that Patsy Devin, in jail for murder, would be lynched too. The mob left him unmolested, though the feeling was very strong.

There are at least two thousand farmers in Anderson county who have given liens this year to secure advances with which to make their crop, and if the law is repealed this winter what will they do next year? It is fair to presume that only those who cannot obtain supplies without liens give them, and why any one should desire to deprive them of its friendly aid is more than we can understand.

The Leader of a Kansas Mob Shot by a Prisoner.

hardin-brothers-fredonia-1881-08-07.A23: New York Tribune: Mob are always cowardly. hardin-brothers-fredonia-1881-08-07.A29:
WESTERN LAWLESSNESS.
Lynching is now so common that it seldom excites general comment; but the lynching of lynchers is not so frequent. The Kansas affair, in which forty masked men overpowered the guards of Fredonia jail, but were put to flight by a pistol handed to one of the prisoners by a guard, with which he shot the leader, shows the folly of lynch law. Hero was a respected, well-to-do farmer killed while breaking the law, in order to expedite justice. Had the two murderers sought by the mob been at large, and had the people, pursuing them, indignant at the sluggishness or connivance of the law, killed them on sight, the affair would have been different; had the jail been thought insecure, and had it therefore been surrounded by a volunteer guard, that also would be intelligible; but the blind fury which wreaks popular vengeance on culprits caught, caged, and awaiting conviction under process of law, needs some such incident as that of Fredonia to expose its senselessless. The mob were really about to commit murder—however the provocation may have seemed to them to justify their act. In addition, they sought to break down the law, and they put its guardians into the dilemma of having to call on jail culprits to help them against the community.

Burglars shot Louis Henir, a New York saloonist, dead, in his house on the night of the 29th ult.

Widow Terrell was shot dead in her own home at Gore, O., on the 28th ult. The murderer was not recognized by Mrs. Terrell's daughters, who were in the house at the time. The victim was the mother of a young man now in the Ohio penitentiary for the murder of the Weldon family near Gore four years ago.

Francisco Alamilla, a Mexican political leader, lying in jail at Humarguillo, was shot without judge or trial.

Johnson revived and dragged himself home, a distance of half a mile. His brother Abe, as deputy sheriff, attempted to secure the assassin and received a fatal wound. In a saloon quarrel at Butte, Montana, Joe Campbell mortally wounded Joe Rowells, of Bodie, Col.

Leon Moore, clerk in a store at Boston, Mass., spent Christmas at his home in Biddeford, Me. On the 26th he called on his affianced, Miss Belle Cushman, an estimable lady, and shot her dead. In a street fight at Eufala, Indian Territory, on the 26th, a carpenter named Ware killed a young man named Grayson. A railway section hand who witnessed the affair became frightened and ran. He was ordered to halt by the police, but refused to comply and was shot dead.

Ole Thompson, a wealthy Norwegian farmer, was found murdered on the farm of his son-in-law on the 27th. The body was horribly mangled. The nephew of the murdered man has disappeared and is supposed to be the murderer.

W. Gibbons. After outraging the young ladies, the fiends killed all three of their victims, saturated their clothing with oil and fired the premises. The house was consumed completely. In a shooting affray at Helenwood, Tenn., on the 25th inst., John Cecil was killed and three brothers named West, W. Smith and a man named Thomson were probably fatally injured.

In a quarrel at Knoxville, Tenn., on the evening of the 24th, the youngest son of Gen. Joseph A. Mabry, was killed by Don Lisby.

The position of the president is an exceedingly delicate one. The independent republicans made his nomination possible at Chicago, but it was the stalwart republicans, under the leadership of Grant, Conkling, Logan, Arthur and Platt, who unattached victory from the very jaws of defeat. That he should feel grateful to both, would be only natural, and that he should seek to unite and harmonize the two factions, would be precisely what everybody would expect and approve. In the character of his appointments thus far, with possibly two exceptions, he has exhibited rare discretion and sound judgment. The country generally was somewhat surprised at his appointment of Stanley Matthews, and it may be—although we are not quite able to see it—that he has erred in nominating Judge Robertson for Collector of the Port of New York. But our senators, in the interest of harmony, can well afford to overlook this latter appointment, inasmuch as the personal fitness of the appointee is universally admitted, and he has been indorsed by the unanimous vote of the senate and assembly of this state.

From the Buffalo Express (Conkling Rep.)

Judge Robertson helped to nominate Garfield; Senator Conkling didn't. Both loyally supported him after his nomination. If the president is forced to choose between them, to which is his obligation the greater? Judge Robertson is no democrat. If he is as good a republican as Senator Conkling, or as President Garfield himself, in what does his deficiency consist? If the president had waited for the senators, the vice president or the postmaster general to suggest for office the name of Judge Robertson, or of any republican of like mind, how long would he probably have had to wait? What reason has President Garfield for excluding Judge Robertson from party recognition? Is the fact that Senator Conkling wants him excluded a sufficient reason? Must the president make the local quarrels of all the senators his own, and punish those who have been and are his friends at another man's bidding?

THE ODDS AGAINST CONKLING.

Syracuse N. Y. Journal (Rep.)

It should be borne in mind that no such division of parties exists in the United States senate as that President Hayes had to deal with. The senate is now a republican body, with the vice-president's casting vote; whereas then it contained a democratic working majority. The senate has been greatly improved by the new men chosen to it the past year. With the single exception of Platt, of New York, all the new republican senators are special friends to Garfield, and not one actively sympathizes with the so-called stalwartism that dominates the politics of this state. The republican reliances of Mr. Conkling have been greatly weakened by the changes which took place on the 4th of March, and not more than four of the present republican senators are peculiarly his allies. On the other hand, Garfield has a positive, and when needed an aggressive, support in the senate, which Hayes never had; and yet Hayes' nomination of Merritt was confirmed! He has, also, warm personal friends among the democratic senators, who, when driven to choose between republicans, will give him all the requisite "advice and consent."

madder-tiffin-1881-11-01.A16:
THE MURDER,
Committed by Charles Madder at Tiffin.
TIFFIN, O., November 7.—The murder of Miss Phebe Bernard by Charles Madder last week has proven to be the most heartrendering tragedy in the history of the city, Madder is a Stark county boy and his family live at East Greenville, about five miles west of Massillon, in Tuscarawas township. Madder was a student at Heidelberg College. Tiffin, and was studying for the ministry. He made the following statement of his crime: We were engaged to be married and she went back on me. I could do nothing, and think of nothing but her. I could neither study nor work, and I resolved to return again and renew my suit. On Wednesnight she refused me again, and I could not get over it. I felt that something must be done, and I got drunk first to give me courage, although it was the first time I ever drank anything stronger than water or coffee since I joined the church. I went to the college while they were taking observations by the telescope, and then waited for her (Phebe) to come along when she went to the party at Sheets, when she came I called her to one side and again requested her to marry me. She refused, and I told her she was the cause of my misery and we would die together. I drew my revolver and cocked it more to make her say yes, than anything else, but somehow the revolver went off, and when she screamed I knew she was shot. I fired the other shots to end her sufferings, and make her stop screaming. My intention was to shoot myself, but try as I would I could not get courage enough to do so. I went to Baldwin's lumber yard and stayed all night, heard the parties in the search, and resolved to give myself up as soon as the excitement died away, and there would be no danger of lynching."

The preliminary examination of Madder, Saturday, was held in the Sheriff's private office, and he was bound over to court for murder in the first degree. Sensational reports of an attempt to lynch Madder have been circulated, but they are all false. Tiffin people are peaceable, and disposed to let the law take its course. Madder was taken from jail last night to Fremont. From thence he will be taken to Toledo in the morning for safe keeping.
madder-tiffin-1881-11-01.A19:
Shocking Murder at Tiffln.
Another shocking murder occurred at Tiffin on Thursday night of last week. A young man named Charles Madder, from Stark county, a student at Heidleberg College, at Tiffin, had been paying attention to and had become infatuated with a bright and handsome young lady, Miss Phoebe Bernard, daughter of a brick mason of that city. It is reported that they were at one time engaged to be married, but that she had broken the engagement after learning that he had occasional symptoms of insanity, and had been sent home for treatment. He had asked her to renew the engagement but she had refused to do so. About 10 o'clock on the fatal night he stepped up to her as she was leaving college chappel, in company with another young lady and gentleman, where they had been attending prayer meeting, and asked to accompany her home, and again renewed his offer of marriage. She again refused and he at once drew a revolver and fired four shots at her, two taking effect in her head, one just below the eye and one in the mouth. Miss Bernard fell and expired in a few moments.

Young Madder who said it was his intention to have completed the tragedy by shooting himself, failed to find the requisite courage to do so and hastily retreated to a lumber yard in the suburbs of the city where he secreted himself during the remainder of the night, while a large delegation of citizens were eagerly searching for him. He gave himself up to the police on Friday for enoon and was hastily hurried to the jail to prevent his being lynched by an infuriated people.

On Sunday night a mob of several hundred citizens of Tiffin gathered at the jail to lynch the murderer, and it was only prevented by herculean efforts of the whole police force, several of whom were severely injured in the attack of the mob. In the mean time the prisoner was covertly taken from the jail by the Sheriff and taken in a carriage across the country to Fremont where he was kept until Monday morning when he was taken to Toledo and lodged in jail to await his trial.
Young Madder was a member of the junior class in college, studying for entrance to the ministry, and is reported to possess more than ordinary abllity and stood high in esteem of both professors and students, by whom he was admired for his brilliant oratorical abilities in the college societies.

A colored Waiter That Barely Escaped Lynching.
MONT EAGLE, TENN., August 8.—Mont Eagle has had a genuine sensation. A colored waiter threw a plate at a pantry maid, a white girl. The affair reached the ears of a dozen or more young mountaineers, and they at once organized themselves into a mob for the purpose of lynching the sable dispenser of viands, and accordingly, between midnight and daylight they entered the waiters' quarters by force and demanded the refactory individual. This demand, created a panic among the twenty-five or thirty other colored waiters and they stamped taking to the brush. The guilty waiter betook himself to the hotel, where he was locked in a room, to prevent the mob from reaching him. He was afterward arraigned before the Recorder and fined $15 50. Every member of the mob was arrested and taken before a Magistrate. On the individual promise of each never to be guilty of a like proceeding again, they were released. The colored waiter was placed on the train at night and sent to Nashville, which is also the home of the pantry maid. J. C. C.

Before he was drawn up, Jennings was heard to say, "Oh, my God! Boys, I guess I deserve this." He then groaned loudly as he was about starting upward. Very shortly after the work was done word was passed down Main street that Jennings had been hanged, and quite a large number of persons gathered to view the body and listen to the story of the Deputy Sheriff. Coroner Laughlin was very shortly on the ground, and in the course of half an hour after the hanging took place that officer cut the rope, and placed the body inside the Sheriff's office, where it lay till this forenoon, when it was taken to the City Hall. The circumstances of the murder which caused Jennings to be lynched are as follows: Monday night Barrett was in the saloon of the International Hotel, when the man Jennings started a quarrel with him for some cause unknown. The quarrel soon ended and the matter seemed settled; but a few minutes later Barrett asked Jennings up to take a drink. The two stood at the bar, and Barrett turned around, while waiting for the drinks, to talk to another person, whereupon Jennings drew a Smith & Wesson self-cocking revolver and fired three shots. One of them entered under the right shoulder-blade and struck the spinal column. Barrett was paralyzed, fell heavily to the floor, and died almost instantly. Barrett, it seems, was not to blame and did everything he could to stave off trouble. The cold-blooded and unprovoked murder excited the bitterest feeling against Jennings. Barrett was generally liked, and his death was deeply regretted. He was an industrious, respectable citizen, 31 years old, having a wife and two children. Jennings had not been in Austin more than two weeks. He is a native of Cornwall, and was looked upon as a quarrelsome fellow. He has a wife and four children living in Grass Valley. The feeling against the murderer grew more and more intense as the deed was discussed, but there was no indication of the purpose to lynch him. Preparations were made quietly, but, as the result shows, very effectively.

IN GENERAL.
Edward Fearing, son of a wealthy resident of New York, committed suicide in Auburn on Sunday night.
Theodore Ahrens, aged 27 years, committed suicide in Baltimore, Sunday morning, by shooting himself in the head.

Eight persons were drowned Thursday at Cincinnati. Six of the victims perished at one time by the upsetting of a skiff.

The census of Halifax, Nova Scotia, just completed, gives that city a population of 36,109, an increase of 6,527 in the last decade.

The Golden Circle Mines, on the Salmon river, in Lemhi county, Idaho, have been bought by English capitalists for $250,000.

Tuesday, being the one hundred and thirty-second anniversary of the founding of Halifax, Nova Scotia, was observed as a holiday in that city.

Rear Admiral George B. Balch, recently detached from the superintendency of the Naval Academy, is ordered to command the Pacific squadron.

During a hail storm at Babylon, Long Island, on Sunday night, hail-stones as large as walnuts fell, smashing windows, and badly damaging the crops.

Harbor Briton lighthouse, in Fortune Bay, Newfoundland, has been destroyed by fire. It will probably be several months before the structure can be replaced.

A young man, named Noble, was shot dead while lying in bed at Chinaville, Ark., last Friday night. The murderer is unknown. It is thought his intention was to kill Noble's father.

Judge Lynch in Butte County—A Murderer Taken from Jail by Citizens and Hanged.

OROVILLE, August 7th.—J. F. Noakes, who murdered A. J. Crum, about three weeks ago, at Chico, was taken from the jail this morning by a posse of armed and masked men, and conveyed to Crum's old place, about ten miles from here, on the road to Chico, and there hanged by the neck to the limb of a large oak tree. The body was first discovered hanging there early this morning by Sheriff Sprague, who was returning home from a business trip to Durham, Coroner Mitchell and a jury are now gone there to hold an inquest and bury the body. Under Sheriff Patten was confined to his bed by illness, and jailer Knowles was the only person at the jail. He was awakened at about 2 A.M. by a knock on the outer door, and in reply to his inquiry of "Who's there?" the answer was made that an officer from Biggs with a prisoner desired admission. The jailer unlocked the door, when it was suddenly pushed wide open and about fifteen masked and armed men crowded into the jailer's room, seized and disarmed him, and demanded the keys of the jail, at the same time telling Knowles who they were after. Knowles refused to disclose where the keys were, and the party at once set to work with tools which they brought with them to break open the doors. Noakes was confined in one of the iron tanks, and the party was apparently well aware which cell he occupied, as they proceeded directly to it, having two wooden and two iron doors to force to reach him. This was accomplished in a very short time, and when his cell door was forced at he once surrendered without any show of resistance. His hands were tied with a rope, and he was placed in a wagon in waiting, with four men standing guard over him, and the whole party drove rapidly away across the river in the direction of Chico. The whole affair was so quickly and quietly accomplished that no alarm whatever was created, and the first any of our citizens knew of it was the alarm given by Jailer Knowles after the party left. They were met on the road a few miles out of town by a person coming in from Pences, and he said he judged there were forty or more in the crowd. t-noakes-oroville-1881-08-07.A13:
THE OROVILLE LYNCHING.
A mob took Thomas Noakes out of jail at Oroville, and hanged him. Noakes had murdered an inoffensive cripple by beating him, and it was undoubtedly a very aggravated and brutal crime. But what reason had the men who murdered Noakes to suppose that the law would not punish him? Every man who joined in that lawless deed has put himself on a par with Noakes. Do they realize this? We are not living here on the frontier beyond the reach of justice. There is no excuse for mob vengeance upon malefactors in California. The brutality of a crime does not afford such an excuse. Those who resort to lynching to satisfy a sentiment of indignation may think that they are justified, but they are wrong. No authority to take life is vested in the citizens, individually or collectively, save in self-defense or under the direct and explicit sanction of the law. In this case, as in all lynchings, one murder has been avenged by another. A lynching is not an execution; it is a murder. There is no sanctifying or exculatory influence about it. It is a mere reckless mob proceeding, and it is one which reflects the deepest discredit upon its participants. And we may add that next to the actual murderers in guilt and responsibility are those public journals which excuse or approve such outrages, no matter under what flimsy pretext. There is but one way to punish crime in a civilized community, and that is through the constituted machinery. All evasions of that machinery but serve to promote lawlessness, whether they are committed with criminal intent, or under the mistaken idea of furthering the ends of justice.

Special Correspondence of The Chicago Tribune.

Wend City, Mo., Aug. 1.—About the year 1852 a friend of mine made a pilgrimage from Henry County, Iowa, into southwest Missouri, peddling looms. He found but few settlers in the region round about Springfield and Carthage; and among the few people living there he did not find a cook-stove or match. To-day Jasper County stands fourth among the Counties of Missouri in point of population. Jasper borders on Kansas, and is two counties from the Arkansas State line. Carthage is the county-seat; and one finds there a beautiful city of 6,000 or more souls, populated by a very thriving people. For the first time in its history Jasper elected all the Republican candidates for county offices in 1880. Yet there is living a bitter feeling of resentment against the "Yankees," as evidenced by a remark I heard while on the streets of Carthage. A number of men were sitting on the outer edge of the sidewalk in front of a hotel, and as I came up even with them, one of the number—a good-looking man, aged probably 60 years—remarked that, "Before the d—d Yankees came into this country, we used to have good times." As to his meaning of good times, I think he meant pleasant times, when their enjoyment with each other was more of the camp-meeting order; for the reasons that Carthage is enjoying a healthy and enduring growth.

Three-fourths of Jasper County is reputed to be very rich in agricultural resources. I never saw finer corn growing in Iowa than is about riponing on all sides of Carthage. There are several very large flour-mills in town, and an extensive hotel is building. Four banks supply the loaning funds of the city. The southwest quarter of Jasper County is wholly given up to stony hills. Going from Iowa, where a stony farm is a curiosity, to the southwest of Jasper County, Missouri, it seemed to me, while driving over the Missouri country-roads in a buggy, that howliders as big as my head were loft right in the wagon-track on purpose for me to practice driving around. And, by the way, there's a peculiar skill requisit for a pleasant drive over those stony hills of Jasper County.

But there is a wealth yet uncomputed lying hidden under those stony hills. At a little place called Oronoco (Oro-or-no-go) lead has been worked out of the ground for some years, and it is yet a busy camp. About 1871-'2-'7 lead was discovered at Joplin, and since then an immenso amount of ore has been taken out there, aggregating millions of dollars' worth. A pretty extensive smelting-works is operating; also, as I am informed, the largest white-lead works in the country is manufacturing. Joplin has a population of 4,000, and presents a very neat appearance for a mining town, and has a number of good business-houses. The most extensive lead-lind there is worked nearly "dry," yet some shafts are drawing out vast quantities. The old mining part of the town presents a deserted appearance,—there not being a sign of a windlass, or crusher, or jig on any of the thousands of dumps scattered over a thousand acres of ground lying adjoining the north of Joplin. Each dump represents a shaft, or where one was started. The lead was, found at all depths, from ten to 100 feet. The smelting-works at Joplin have a capacity of 25,000 pounds of mineral per day.

just as the last peals of the tolling bells were resounding throughout the city, the sharp crack of a pistol was heard in the rear of the "den" (we can give it no other name as it is an intolerable nuisance) at the head of Milam street, known as the Red store. As quickly as possible a large crowd assembled to know the cause, and the only mark left was Aaron White, a well known colored boy, an employee of the barber-shops, lying on the ground weltering in blood flowing from a dangerous wound he had received from a pistol ball. Police Officer McRady passed quickly out of the door and made his way toward the station house, where he armed himself as best he could and accompanied by Mr. J. R. Herndon, started in pursuit of the guilty parties. Everything was excitement and it was some time before we were enabled to find out the facts in the case. We had our reportorial augur with us, however, and were just as determined as ever we were in our life, to learn facts, particularly when when we heard a short time later that one of the partier engaged in the trouble had been shot dead by the officer. A little patience and diligence put us in possession of the following facts, which were established before the Mayor's court yesterday morning:

It seems that some difficulty occurred to the saloon in rear of the Red store between Eliza Jackson, a colored woman of bad repute and a colored steamboat roustabout named Wm. Bowie, in which some rough words passed. The woman appealed to Mr. McRady, who is the policeman on the beat, to arrest the man for being disorderly and abusing her. Mr. McRady entered the saloon, and as there were two or three colored men sitting around asked her to point out the man and she pointed out Bowie. He took Bowie by the arm and told him to consider himself under arrest and go with him to the station. Bowie said something about getting his shoes which were in a house some distance off, but the officer told him he could get them afterward, when another colored man sitting in the room, named Abe Johnson, commenced interfering with the officer, and he, McRady, told him if he didn't keep quiet he would arrest him.

Johnson said he be d—d if he would, there wasn't policemen enough in Shreveport to arrest him; and used other harsh language. He also said something about Bowie being crippled. Officer McRady then let go of Bowie and took hold of Johnson, who is a very stout man, and scuffled with him, calling on Elbridge Geary and Aaron White, two colored men, to assist him in making the arrest. The prisoner threw Geary aside as "if he were a boy," to use his own language before the mayor's court, and continued his scuffle with Officer McRady, calling to his frisnd Bowie to grab his (McRady's) pistol and shoot the d—d police s—n of a b—h. Policeman McRady of Shreveport, who killed Wm. Bowie, a colored desperado, in self defense, has been exonerated from blame.

J. D. Hines and R. McIntash had a difficulty at Cottonport, and the latter was shot and slightly wounded. Hines is in jail.

A man charged with stealing a duck spent fifty-three days in the jail of Concordia parish and was then set at liberty without a trial.

A colored thief who robbed the residence of Mr. Randolph Snyder, near Port Hudson, has been captured. His name is Henry Hansey.

Alexandria anticipates having railroad communication with New Orleans via the N. O. Pacific and Morgan lines, ere the end of the current month.

Jeff Harris, colored, shot and killed Henderson Jackson, also colored, near Athens. The killing is looked upon as wilful murder. Harris is at large.

John Williams, colored, was waylaid and shot to death in Bossier parish, and Jack Chapman, also colored, is in jail at Bellevue charged with the assassination.

A colored citizen of Baton Rouge replenished his exchequer by going about with a spade on his shoulder soliciting subscriptions to bury a man who was not dead.

Six hands on the Lusk plantation, in Terrebonne parish, struck for higher wages and refusing to resume work or leave the place, were ejected by the Sheriff.

The steam gin on the Downing & Merrick plantation on Bayou Fordoche, Pointe Conpée parish, was destroyed by fire. There was no insurance on the property.

Dave Robinson, a cotton picker in Caddo parish, had his arm so badly mangled in a cotton gin that amputation was necessary. His condition is critical.

Mr. Spicer Jones successfully experimented in the manufacture of sugar from pumpkins on Mr. Marcelin Tircuit's place, St. James parish, and proposes to patent the process.

Eight head of cattle belonging to Mr. DeFee, in East Carroll parish, broke into a cotton field where worm destroyer had been used and were fatally poisoned from grazing there.

Charlie Johnson, who recently murdered Squire Coleman near Shreveport, after enticing Coleman's wife to leave him, has been sentenced to life imprisonment in the penitentiary.
A pecan tree in Thibodaux over 100 years old that ceased to bear was made to yield again by boring a hole in its trunk and driving the limb of a young pecan tree into the aperture.

On the Marshall place, in Madison parish, John Boyd had a difficulty with several colored men and stabbed three of them with a knife. One of the wounded men subsequently died.

The planters of St. Mary parish have formed an association and decided to pay laborers during the approaching grinding season $1.50 and rations for eighteen hours work, or $1.75 without rations.

The store of Mr. Lazarus Mayer, in Harrisonburg was destroyed by fire which is believed to have been set by an incendiary. Mr. Mayer's residence, fifty feet away, was saved with great difficulty.

A flat car and the caboose of a construction train on the New Orleans Pacific railroad ran off the track en route from Mansfield to Shreveport. A white man named Wm. E. Wood was run over and instantly killed.

Mr. Wm. Vaughan, who was waylaid and shot by some unknown scoundrel, in the parish of Caddo, seems to be in a fair way to recover from his wounds. A reward of $260 is offered for the detection of his would be assassin.

A building used as a cooper, carpenter and blacksmith shop was burned on Mr. Gibson's Greenwood plantation, Terrebonne parish. The fine sugar-house, standing only thirty yards distant, narrowly escaped destruction.
The gin-house and wheelwright shop of Mr. Chas. Wyland, situated nine miles from Baton Rouge, were destroyed by fire last week, together with thirty-two tons of cotton seed, a wagon, a buggy and all of Mr. Wyland's tools. No insurance.
